steps.title: A prediction engine
steps.text: An AI model is a prediction engine trained on a huge amount of text (and often images, audio and video). You give it input, and it predicts the most useful continuation, one small piece at a time.

steps.title: Your mental model
steps.text: Treat it like a brilliant, fast new hire who has read everything but knows nothing about you. Your job is to brief it.

steps.question: What does a model actually do with your prompt?
options: Looks the answer up in a database
Predicts the most useful continuation, piece by piece
steps.explain: It predicts, which is why it can sound sure and still be wrong.

steps.statement: A model already knows about your business and goals.
steps.explain: It knows nothing about you until you brief it.

steps.title: Tokens
steps.text: A token is a chunk of text, roughly ¾ of a word. Usage limits and API prices are counted in tokens, e.g. "$2 per 1M tokens in".

steps.title: Context window
steps.text: The context window is how much the model can "see" at once: your prompt, the chat so far and any files. Bigger windows fit whole books or codebases.

steps.question: Roughly what is a token?
options: A chunk of text, about ¾ of a word
steps.explain: Prices and limits are counted in tokens.

steps.statement: If you paste a 300-page PDF, you can assume the model read every line carefully.

steps.title: Hallucination
steps.text: A confident answer that is simply wrong or made up. Always ask for sources and check the numbers that matter.

steps.title: Reasoning, multimodal, open weights
steps.text: Reasoning mode thinks step by step first: slower, better on hard problems. Multimodal means it takes or makes images, audio or video. Open weights are models you can download and run yourself.

steps.prompt: Match each word to its meaning
pairs: Thinks step by step before answering
Handles images, audio or video too
A model you can run yourself

steps.question: When is reasoning mode worth the wait?
options: Planning a multi-step project or tricky math
steps.explain: Reasoning helps on hard, multi-step problems.

steps.title: One main assistant
steps.text: You don't need every model. You need one main assistant, plus a sense of which specialist to grab for images, video or voice.

steps.title: Specialists
steps.text: Media tools are specialists: image models for thumbnails and product shots, video models for ads and shorts, voice models for narration and voice agents.

steps.statement: A good starting move is paying for three $20 plans on day one.
steps.explain: Start free, upgrade the one you hit limits on daily.

steps.title: The big families (checked Oct 14, 2026)
steps.text: Grok: coding, agents, live X/web search and news. Claude: writing, long documents, coding agents. GPT/ChatGPT: everyday all-rounder and image generation. Gemini: Google Workspace, 1M context, research. Open weights (Qwen, DeepSeek, Gemma…): privacy, running locally, low cost at volume.
steps.note: Prices and names change weekly. Re-check before you buy.

steps.prompt: Match the family to what it's best at

steps.statement: Sora is still the best video model to start with.
steps.explain: Sora was shut down in 2026 (app Apr 26, API Sep 24).

steps.title: Quick picker
steps.text: Writing & long docs → Claude. Live news & X → Grok. Google apps & huge docs → Gemini. All-rounder → ChatGPT. Private / local → open weights. Bulk cheap steps → small fast models like Haiku, Luna or DeepSeek Flash.

steps.question: You want news from the last 24 hours on X. Which family is strongest?
steps.explain: Live X/web search is Grok's differentiator.

steps.question: Privacy-sensitive data that must stay on your machine?
steps.explain: Open weights can run on your own hardware.

steps.title: Four parts of a good prompt
steps.text: Most "AI is bad" moments are briefing problems.

steps.question: Which prompt will get a better caption?
steps.a: Write an Instagram caption for my bakery.
steps.b: You're a social media copywriter for a small Portland bakery. Goal: pre-orders of pumpkin croissants for Saturday. Write 3 captions under 40 words, max 2 emojis, ending with "Pre-order via link in bio".
steps.explain: Role, goal, audience and format beat a one-liner.

steps.prompt: Put the fix-it loop in order
items: Keep the rule for next time

steps.title: Adjectives are where the default look lives
steps.text: Replace "nice", "premium", "engaging" with counts, sizes, angles, word limits and examples.

steps.question: Which product-photo prompt is stronger?
steps.a: Product shot of a matte black bottle on wet slate. 85mm, eye level, f/2.8, bottle fills 60% of frame. One softbox 45° left, warm rim light. 4:5, no text.
steps.b: Make my product photo look premium and cinematic.

steps.question: Which change improves a prompt most?
options: Replacing adjectives with concrete numbers and an example

steps.title: Build it up
steps.text: A weak prompt gets strong when you add a role, a goal, constraints and a format. Examples lock the style.

steps.base: Write a product description for my candle.

chips.label: Role
chips.text: You are a copywriter for an eco home brand.

chips.label: Goal
chips.text: Goal: get Etsy shoppers to add it to cart.

steps.explain: Role, goal and format help. Shouting doesn't.

steps.question: The draft is too long and too formal. Best follow-up?
options: 'Cut to 50 words, casual tone, like this example: …'
Start a new chat with the same prompt
steps.explain: Name the exact problem and the target.
